nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the autobiographical epic of American appetite and the lyric of the road
literary_identity: Novelist; the great lyric novelist of American hunger and memory, the author of Look Homeward, Angel and Of Time and the River.
biography: Born Thomas Clayton Wolfe in Asheville, North Carolina, on 3 October 1900; he read at the University of North Carolina and took a Harvard degree in playwriting, taught at New York University from 1924, and published Look Homeward, Angel in 1929 — a novel of his own family and town that caused a scandal in Asheville. Of Time and the River (1935), The Web and the Rock (1939) and You Can't Go Home Again (1940) followed, the last two edited posthumously from his manuscripts by Edward Aswell. He died of tuberculosis in Baltimore on 15 September 1938, aged thirty-seven.
literary_profile: Wolfe wrote the great lyric epic of American appetite: Look Homeward, Angel and Of Time and the River are the most expansive autobiographical novels in American literature, and their torrent of names, foods, places and memories made a new kind of American prose. His subject — the small town, the family, the hunger to escape and the impossibility of return — is the central American subject of the period, and he is the missing link between the Southern Renaissance and the Beat generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The long catalogue of names, objects and sensations; the lyric passage that swells beyond its subject; the autobiographical protagonist (Eugene Gant); the obsessive family portrait; the run-on sentence and the rhetorical apostrophe; the prose poem of the American night.
intellectual_concerns: The American small town and the family; hunger, appetite and the desire for experience; the South and the escape from it; memory, loss and the impossibility of return; the artist's formation; the American road and the American night.
historical_significance: Wolfe wrote the most expansive autobiographical novel in American literature and the great lyric record of American appetite: Look Homeward, Angel and Of Time and the River changed the possibilities of American prose, his portrait of the Southern family is permanent, and his influence runs through Kerouac and the Beats.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Look Homeward, Angel (1929); Of Time and the River (1935); From Death to Morning (1935, stories); The Story of a Novel (1936, essay); The Web and the Rock (1939, posthumous); You Can't Go Home Again (1940, posthumous); The Hills Beyond (1941, posthumous); The Letters of Thomas Wolfe (1956, posthumous); The Notebooks of Thomas Wolfe (1970, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the short story as a perfected form and the Southern family of memory
literary_identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest American short-story writer of the period, the author of Flowering Judas and Ship of Fools.
biography: Born Callie Russell Porter at Indian Creek, Texas, on 15 May 1890; she was raised by her grandmother in Texas and Louisiana, married young and divorced, worked as a journalist in Chicago, Denver and Mexico, and published her first stories in the 1920s. Flowering Judas appeared in 1930, Pale Horse, Pale Rider in 1939, The Leaning Tower in 1944 and the novel Ship of Fools in 1962, which became a best-seller and a film. She won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award in 1966 and died in Silver Spring, Maryland, on 18 September 1980.
literary_profile: Porter wrote the most perfectly finished American short stories of the period: 'Flowering Judas', 'The Jilting of Granny Weatherall', 'Noon Wine' and 'Pale Horse, Pale Rider' are the finest stories in American literature between Anderson and Cheever, and their compression, their exactness of detail and their moral seriousness made the story a form for grown-up art. Ship of Fools is the great American novel of the 1930s' political shipwreck.
stylistic_characteristics: The story built on a single scene and a single revelation; the exact material detail (the food, the clothes, the room); the free indirect style that enters a mind without breaking; the retrospective frame of memory; the unemphatic, perfectly weighted ending.
intellectual_concerns: Memory and the lost Southern childhood; the family and the grandmother; love, betrayal and the jilting; illness, death and the influenza epidemic; Mexico and the revolutionary expatriate; the ship, the voyage and the political exile.
historical_significance: Porter wrote the finest American short stories of the period and the great American novel of the 1930s: Flowering Judas and Pale Horse, Pale Rider set the standard for the modern story, her childhood stories of Texas and Louisiana preserve a lost world, and Ship of Fools is a permanent record of the decade's political despair.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Flowering Judas (1930, stories); Noon Wine (1937, novella); Pale Horse, Pale Rider (1939, three novellas); The Leaning Tower and Other Stories (1944); The Days Before (1952, essays); Ship of Fools (1962, novel); The Collected Stories of Katherine Anne Porter (1965); A Christmas Story (1967); The Never-Ending Wrong (1977, essay); 'The Jilting of Granny Weatherall' (1930); 'Flowering Judas' (1930); 'The Grave' (1935); 'He' (1927); 'Maria Concepción' (1922).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the comic-grotesque Southern story and the novel of the small town
literary_identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest comic writer of the Southern Renaissance and the author of A Curtain of Green and The Optimist's Daughter.
biography: Born Eudora Alice Welty in Jackson, Mississippi, on 13 April 1909; she studied at Mississippi State College for Women, the University of Wisconsin and Columbia, worked as a publicity agent for the WPA in Mississippi in the 1930s — photographing the rural poor — and published A Curtain of Green in 1941. The Robber Bridegroom (1942), Delta Wedding (1946), The Ponder Heart (1954), The Optimist's Daughter (1972, Pulitzer Prize) and One Writer's Beginnings (1984) followed. She died in Jackson on 23 July 2001.
literary_profile: Welty wrote the finest comic fiction of the Southern Renaissance: her stories of the Mississippi small town and the rural poor — 'A Worn Path', 'Why I Live at the P.O.', 'Petrified Man' — made the grotesque funny without condescension, and her novels of the Mississippi family are the warmest in the Southern tradition. Her photographs of the Depression South are a documentary record of equal importance.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic monologue and the first-person eccentric voice; the story built on a single comic situation; the precise rendering of dialect without caricature; the fairy-tale and folk-tale structure (The Robber Bridegroom); the lyric description of the Mississippi landscape.
intellectual_concerns: The Mississippi small town and its eccentrics; the family, the wedding and the funeral; race and the Southern social order; the rural poor and the Depression; the comic survival of the isolated woman; memory and the return home.
historical_significance: Welty is the great comic writer of the Southern Renaissance and the finest American short-story writer of her generation: A Curtain of Green and The Wide Net are permanent, The Optimist's Daughter won the Pulitzer Prize, and her photographs and memoir made her the period's most humane Southern witness.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Southern Gothic of adolescence and the novel of the solitary heart
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and playwright; the author of The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter, written at twenty-three, and the youngest of the great Southern writers.
biography: Born Lula Carson Smith in Columbus, Georgia, on 19 February 1917; she went to New York at seventeen to study music, worked in a variety of jobs, and published The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter in 1940 at the age of twenty-three. Reflections in a Golden Eye (1941), The Member of the Wedding (1946) and The Ballad of the Sad Café (1951) followed, together with the play The Square Root of Wonderful (1958); she suffered strokes and illness through her adult life and died at Nyack, New York, on 29 September 1967.
literary_profile: McCullers wrote the most haunting Southern novel of adolescence: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter made deafness, loneliness and the small Georgia mill town into a great American subject, and The Member of the Wedding is one of the finest American novels of a girl's growing up. Her Gothic of the solitary heart — the freak, the outsider, the unloved — is the period's distinctive contribution to the Southern tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, bare, exactly observed sentence; the grotesque character rendered without condescension; the novel of adolescence and the single summer; the symbolic situation (the deaf mute, the wedding, the café); the loneliness that is never explained.
intellectual_concerns: Loneliness and the solitary heart; adolescence and the desire to belong; race and the Southern town; the freak, the outsider and the migrant worker; deafness, speech and the failure of communication; love as a thing that is not returned.
historical_significance: McCullers wrote the most haunting Southern novel of adolescence and one of the finest American novels of loneliness: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter, written at twenty-three, is a permanent American classic, The Member of the Wedding a great novel of growing up, and The Ballad of the Sad Café a perfect Gothic novella.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter (1940, novel); Reflections in a Golden Eye (1941, novel); The Member of the Wedding (1946, novel; play 1950); The Ballad of the Sad Café (1951, novella and stories); The Square Root of Wonderful (1958, play); Clock Without Hands (1961, novel); Sweet as a Pickle and Clean as a Pig (1964, poems); The Mortgaged Heart (1971, posthumous); Illumination and Night Glare (1999, posthumous autobiography).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the thirties public poem, the elegy and the poetry of the modern city
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the central English poet of the 1930s, the leader of the Auden generation, and one of the great public poets of the century.
biography: Born Wystan Hugh Auden in York on 21 February 1907, the son of a physician; he read at Christ Church, Oxford, where his Poems (1928, privately printed by Spender) and Poems (1930) made him the leader of his generation. The Orators (1932), Look, Stranger! (1936), the plays with Isherwood (The Dog Beneath the Skin, 1935; The Ascent of F6, 1936; On the Frontier, 1938) and Journey to a War (1939) made him the voice of the decade; he emigrated to America in 1939, became an American citizen in 1946, and returned to Oxford as professor of poetry (1956–61). He died in Vienna on 29 September 1973.
literary_profile: Auden is the central English poet of the 1930s and one of the great poets of the century: he gave the decade its public voice — the clipped, journalistic line, the parable, the political fable — and then, in America, wrote the great religious and meditative poems ('In Memory of W. B. Yeats', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'September 1, 1939', the Christmas oratorio For the Time Being). His technical range — ballad, sonnet, sestina, haiku, libretto, light verse — is unmatched in modern English poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: The clipped journalistic line with the flat technical vocabulary; the rhymed parable and the nursery-rhyme turned political; the catalogue of places and machines; the public elegy; the sudden turn from satire to tenderness; the colloquial idiom held in strict form.
intellectual_concerns: Totalitarianism and the coming war; class, the public school and the English ruling order; love, anxiety and the divided self; the modern city, the aeroplane and the machine; faith, the Church and the possibility of belief; history and the individual's place in it.
historical_significance: Auden is the central English poet of the period after Eliot: he gave the thirties its public voice, invented the political poem as a modern form, wrote the great elegies and meditations of the century, and his technical range made him the model for every English poet since. He is the period's most influential poet after Eliot and Yeats.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the Berlin novel, the documentary report and the autobiography of a generation
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and memoirist; the author of Goodbye to Berlin and Berlin Stories, the source of Cabaret, and the closest collaborator of Auden.
biography: Born Christopher William Bradshaw-Isherwood at Disley, Cheshire, on 26 August 1904; he read at Cambridge, left without a degree, worked as a tutor and a secretary, and went to Berlin in 1929, where he taught English and wrote The Last of Mr Norris (1935) and Goodbye to Berlin (1939). He collaborated with Auden on three plays, emigrated to America in 1939, worked in Hollywood as a screenwriter, became a Hindu monk and the disciple of Swami Prabhavananda, translated the Bhagavad Gita, and wrote the autobiographical Lions and Shadows (1938) and Christopher and His Kind (1976). He died at Santa Monica on 4 January 1986.
literary_profile: Isherwood's Berlin novels are the finest English record of the Weimar Republic's last years: Goodbye to Berlin gave the period its image of the doomed city and its narrator's famous 'I am a camera', and the two Berlin books became the musical Cabaret. His documentaries — Journey to a War with Auden, The Condor and the Cows — and his frank autobiography made him the period's great witness and one of the first English writers to write openly about homosexuality.
stylistic_characteristics: The camera-eye narration: the observer who records without comment; the flat, exact, unadorned sentence; the scene assembled from dialogue and detail; the documentary report with the novelist's eye; the self-deprecating autobiographical confidence.
intellectual_concerns: Berlin and the collapse of the Weimar Republic; the rise of the Nazis and the political emergency; the expatriate and the Englishman abroad; homosexuality and the double life; the documentary witness and the artist's responsibility; India, religion and the search for a teacher.
historical_significance: Isherwood wrote the definitive English book about Weimar Berlin and one of the great documentaries of the period: Goodbye to Berlin gave the thirties its image of the doomed city, the Berlin stories became Cabaret, and Christopher and His Kind made him a pioneer of gay autobiography.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the thirties lyric, the political poem and the poetry of the Spanish war
literary_identity: Poet, essayist and editor; one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the editor of Horizon and Encounter.
biography: Born Stephen Harold Spender in London on 28 February 1909, the son of a journalist; he read at University College, Oxford, where he printed Auden's first book, and published Twenty Poems (1930), Poems (1933), Vienna (1934) and The Still Centre (1939). He joined the Communist Party briefly in 1937, served in the National Fire Service in the war, edited Horizon with Cyril Connolly (1939–41) and Encounter (1953–67), taught at American universities, and died in London on 16 July 1995.
literary_profile: Spender is the lyric poet of the Auden generation: 'The Pylons', 'The Express', 'Not Palaces' and 'I Think Continually of Those Who Were Truly Great' are the finest poems of the thirties' public manner, and his Spanish Civil War poems gave the decade its conscience. As editor of Horizon and Encounter he made the period's literary conversation, and his autobiography World Within World is one of the great English memoirs of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The lyric line held in traditional stanza; the aeroplane, the pylon and the machine as symbols of the future; the political statement made in the first person; the elegy for the dead of Spain; the autobiographical prose of a generation.
intellectual_concerns: The thirties and the coming war; the Spanish Civil War; the machine, the pylon and the modern landscape; love, homosexuality and the private life; the artist's politics and the betrayal of the cause; memory and the lost generation.
historical_significance: Spender is one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the period's great editor: 'The Pylons' and 'Not Palaces' are the finest poems of the thirties' public style, his Spanish war poems gave the decade its conscience, and Horizon and Encounter made him the period's principal literary editor.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-British; the thirties poem of the ordinary and the elegy of the modern city
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and radio writer; the finest poet of the Auden generation after Auden, the author of Autumn Journal, and the period's great writer for radio.
biography: Born Frederick Louis MacNeice in Belfast on 12 September 1907, the son of a clergyman; his mother died when he was six and he was sent to school in England, reading classics at Oxford and lecturing in classics at Birmingham and London. Blind Fireworks (1929), Poems (1935) and Autumn Journal (1939) made his name; he worked for the BBC from 1941 as a writer and producer of radio features, translated Aeschylus and Goethe, and died in London on 3 September 1963.
literary_profile: MacNeice is the most individual poet of the Auden generation: Autumn Journal — a long poem of the months from autumn 1938 to the spring of 1939 — is the finest poetic diary of the period, and 'Bagpipe Music', 'Snow' and 'The Sunlight on the Garden' are among the best-loved poems of the century. As a BBC writer he invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism (Modern Poetry, 1938) is the sharpest account of what the thirties were doing.
stylistic_characteristics: The long conversational poem in sections; the rhyme that falls with comic exactness; the catalogue of ordinary things (the bicycle, the pub, the newspaper); the classical and the modern held side by side; the radio script's montage of voices and sound.
intellectual_concerns: The thirties and the coming war; Belfast, Ireland and the divided inheritance; the ordinary English life and the objects of the modern city; time, love and the transience of everything; the classics and the modern world; the provinces and the metropolis.
historical_significance: MacNeice wrote the finest long poem of the thirties in Autumn Journal and the best-loved lyrics of the Auden generation, invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism gives the period its clearest account of itself. He is the most individual and the most durable poet of his group.
